summary.text: For \(m=39101\), the number \(N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1\) is proved prime by an \(N+1\) certificate in the quadratic algebra \(\theta^2=4\theta-1\pmod N\): explicit modular exponentiations and unit checks force every prime divisor \(r\mid N\) to satisfy \(3^{39101}\mid r-1\) or \(3^{39101}\mid r+1\), while \(N<(3^{39101}-1)^2\) rules out compositeness. Hence \(m=39101\) supplies a positive witness, so the defining set is nonempty and its least element cannot be zero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 n_0=100943,\qquad m_0=39101,
\]
and put
\[
 q=3^{39101},\qquad N=2n_0q-1=201886\cdot 3^{39101}-1.
\]
We shall prove that \(N\) is prime. It will then follow immediately that \(m_0\) is one of the positive exponents occurring in the definition of A354747, and hence that \(a(100943)\neq 0\).

The primality proof is an \(N+1\) argument in a quadratic algebra. We first establish the general criterion that is used, then describe and apply the finite certificate for this particular \(N\).

## 1. The quadratic algebra

For a commutative ring \(R\) and an element \(p\in R\), let
\[
 A_p(R)=R[\theta]/(\theta^2-p\theta+1).
\]
Every element can be represented uniquely in the form \(a+b\theta\), and multiplication is
\[
 (a+b\theta)(c+d\theta)
   =(ac-bd)+(ad+bc+pbd)\theta,
\]
because \(\theta^2=p\theta-1\).

Define
\[
 \bar\theta=p-\theta.
\]
Then
\[
 \theta\bar\theta=\theta(p-\theta)=p\theta-(p\theta-1)=1.
\]
Thus \(\theta\) is a unit with inverse \(\bar\theta\). Also
\[
 \theta+\bar\theta=p.
\]

We will principally use this algebra with \(R=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\), and later with \(R=\mathbb F_r\) for a prime divisor \(r\) of \(N\).

## 2. A finite-field order dichotomy

We need the following fact.

**Lemma.** Let \(r\) be prime, let \(p\in\mathbb F_r\), and suppose
\[
 p^2-4\neq 0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_r.
\]
In \(A_p(\mathbb F_r)\), one has
\[
 \theta^{r-1}=1\qquad\text{or}\qquad \theta^{r+1}=1.
\]

**Proof.** The defining equation of \(\theta\) is
\[
 \theta^2-p\theta+1=0.
\]
In characteristic \(r\), taking \(r\)-th powers and using the Frobenius identity \((x+y)^r=x^r+y^r\) gives
\[
 (\theta^r)^2-p\theta^r+1=0,
\]
since \(p^r=p\) in \(\mathbb F_r\). Therefore \(\theta^r\) is also a root of the same quadratic. As the two formal roots in the quadratic algebra are \(\theta\) and \(\bar\theta=p-\theta\), this yields the factorization
\[
 (\theta^r-\theta)(\theta^r-\bar\theta)=0. \tag{1}
\]
Multiplying the first factor by \(\bar\theta=\theta^{-1}\), and the second by \(\theta\), transforms (1) into
\[
 (\theta^{r-1}-1)(\theta^{r+1}-1)=0. \tag{2}
\]
The algebra need not always be an integral domain, so we must justify that (2) implies the desired alternative. There are two cases.

### Split case

Suppose the polynomial
\[
 X^2-pX+1
\]
has a root \(u\in\mathbb F_r\). Its other root is
\[
 u'=p-u.
\]
The product of the roots is \(uu'=1\), so both \(u\) and \(u'\) are nonzero. They are distinct: if \(u=u'\), then \(p=2u\), and substituting this into \(u^2-pu+1=0\) gives \(p^2-4=0\), contrary to the hypothesis.

Evaluation at either root gives a ring homomorphism
\[
 A_p(\mathbb F_r)\longrightarrow \mathbb F_r,
 \qquad a+b\theta\longmapsto a+bu
\]
(and similarly with \(u'\)). Let
\[
 x=\theta^{r-1}=a+b\theta.
\]
By Fermat's theorem, \(u^{r-1}=1\) and \((u')^{r-1}=1\). Evaluating \(x\) at the two roots gives
\[
 a+bu=1,\qquad a+bu'=1.
\]
Subtracting, we obtain
\[
 b(u-u')=0.
\]
Since \(u\neq u'\), it follows that \(b=0\), and then \(a=1\). Hence \(x=1\), so in the split case
\[
 \theta^{r-1}=1.
\]

### Nonsplit case

Suppose instead that \(X^2-pX+1\) has no root in \(\mathbb F_r\). We show that every nonzero element of \(A_p(\mathbb F_r)\) is a unit.

For \(x=a+b\theta\), define its conjugate by
\[
 \bar x=a+b(p-\theta)=(a+pb)-b\theta.
\]
A direct multiplication gives
\[
 x\bar x=a^2+pab+b^2\in\mathbb F_r. \tag{3}
\]
If the scalar on the right of (3) were zero and \(b\neq0\), then
\[
 u=-a/b
\]
would satisfy
\[
 u^2-pu+1=0,
\]
contradicting nonsplitting. If \(b=0\), equation (3) reduces to \(a^2=0\), so \(a=0\). Thus the norm in (3) vanishes only when \(x=0\). Consequently, if \(x\neq0\), then its norm is a nonzero scalar and
\[
 x^{-1}=\bar x/(a^2+pab+b^2).
\]
Hence the algebra is a field in this case.

Now apply this to (2). If \(\theta^{r-1}-1=0\), then \(\theta^{r-1}=1\). Otherwise the first factor is a unit, so the second factor must vanish, giving \(\theta^{r+1}=1\). This proves the lemma in both cases. \(\square\)

## 3. The general \(N+1\) criterion

We now prove the particular form of the \(N+1\) criterion needed here.

**Proposition.** Let \(N>1\), let \(p\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\), and let \(m\ge1\). Suppose that in \(A_p(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)\):

1. \(\theta^{N+1}=1\);
2. the coefficient of \(\theta\) in \(\theta^{(N+1)/3}\) is a unit modulo \(N\);
3. \(p^2-4\) is a unit modulo \(N\);
4. \(3^m\mid N+1\);
5. \(N<(3^m-1)^2\).

Then \(N\) is prime.

**Proof.** Let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). Reduction modulo \(r\) maps
\[
 A_p(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)
 \longrightarrow A_{p_r}(\mathbb F_r),

a+b\theta\longmapsto \bar a+\bar b\theta,
\]
where \(p_r\) is the reduction of \(p\) modulo \(r\).

The identity \(\theta^{N+1}=1\) remains true after this reduction. Thus the multiplicative order \(d\) of \(\theta\) in the algebra over \(\mathbb F_r\) is defined and satisfies
\[
 d\mid N+1. \tag{4}
\]

The coefficient of \(\theta\) in \(\theta^{(N+1)/3}\) is a unit modulo \(N\), so its image modulo every divisor \(r\) of \(N\) is nonzero. If \(\theta^{(N+1)/3}=1\) after reduction modulo \(r\), its \(\theta\)-coefficient would be zero, a contradiction. Hence
\[
 \theta^{(N+1)/3}\neq1,
\]
and therefore
\[
 d\nmid (N+1)/3. \tag{5}
\]

From (4) and (5), the exponent of \(3\) dividing \(d\) must equal the exponent of \(3\) dividing \(N+1\). Indeed, if \(d\mid N+1\) had at least one fewer factor of \(3\), then all prime-power exponents in \(d\) would be bounded by those in \((N+1)/3\), and hence \(d\mid(N+1)/3\), contrary to (5). Since \(3^m\mid N+1\), it follows that
\[
 3^m\mid d. \tag{6}
\]

The unit condition on \(p^2-4\) also survives reduction modulo \(r\), so \(p_r^2-4\neq0\) in \(\mathbb F_r\). By the finite-field lemma,
\[
 \theta^{r-1}=1\qquad\text{or}\qquad\theta^{r+1}=1.
\]
The order \(d\) therefore divides \(r-1\) or \(r+1\). Combining this with (6), we obtain
\[
 3^m\mid r-1\qquad\text{or}\qquad 3^m\mid r+1. \tag{7}
\]
In either case,
\[
 r\ge 3^m-1. \tag{8}
\]
For the first case, \(r-1\) is a positive multiple of \(3^m\), so in fact \(r\ge3^m+1\); for the second, \(r+1\ge3^m\), giving the displayed weaker bound.

Suppose now that \(N\) were composite, and let \(r\) be its least prime factor. Then \(r^2\le N\): writing \(N=rs\), minimality of \(r\) implies \(s\ge r\). But (8) gives
\[
 (3^m-1)^2\le r^2\le N,
\]
contradicting hypothesis 5. Therefore \(N\) is prime. \(\square\)

## 4. The concrete certificate for \(N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1\)

We apply the proposition with
\[
 p=4,\qquad m=39101.
\]
Thus all arithmetic in this section is in
\[
 A_4(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z),\qquad \theta^2=4\theta-1.
\]

For completeness, the finite modular computation underlying the certificate can be described exactly as follows. Represent \(a+b\theta\) by the pair \((a,b)\), with both entries reduced to \(\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\). Define
\[
 (a,b)\star(c,d)
 =\bigl(ac-bd,\ ad+bc+4bd\bigr)\pmod N. \tag{9}
\]
Starting from \((0,1)\), one cubing step replaces a pair \(x\) by
\[
 C(x)=(x\star x)\star x. \tag{10}
\]
Consequently, after \(k\) iterations,
\[
 C^k(0,1)
\]
represents \(\theta^{3^k}\). This follows inductively: it is true for \(k=0\), and each application of \(C\) cubes the represented element and therefore multiplies its exponent by \(3\).

The accepted certificate computed these iterates in blocks of 460 cubings: first \(C^{460}(0,1)\), then \(C^{920}(0,1)\), and so on through \(C^{39100}(0,1)\), followed by one final cubing to obtain \(C^{39101}(0,1)\). Every block is obtained by repeated use of the explicit multiplication (9), reducing both coordinates modulo \(N\) after each operation.

The remaining exponent \(201886\) is handled by ordinary binary exponentiation using the same multiplication \(\star\): initialize the accumulator to \((1,0)\), repeatedly square the base, multiply the accumulator by the base when the current binary digit of the exponent is 1, and divide the remaining exponent by 2. Thus the computation is entirely a finite sequence of integer additions, multiplications, divisions with remainder, and reductions modulo the explicitly defined integer \(N\).

The two resulting modular identities are
\[
 \left(C^{39101}(0,1)\right)^{\star 201886}=(1,0), \tag{11}
\]
and
\[
 \left(C^{39100}(0,1)\right)^{\star 201886}=(A,B), \tag{12}
\]
where the same finite computation, followed by the Euclidean algorithm, gives
\[
 \gcd(B,N)=1. \tag{13}
\]
Here \(x^{\star e}\) denotes exponentiation with the multiplication (9). Equations (11)--(13) are precisely the mathematical content of the large modular certificate: (11) is the identity check, while (12)--(13) are the nontriviality check one factor of 3 lower. The block computations at exponents \(460,920,\ldots,39100,39101\) serve as intermediate checks of the repeated-cubing chain, and binary exponentiation supplies the final multiplier \(201886\).

Now
\[
 N+1=201886\cdot3^{39101}. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(C^{39101}(0,1)\) represents \(\theta^{3^{39101}}\), equation (11), together with (14), gives
\[
 \theta^{N+1}
 =\left(\theta^{3^{39101}}\right)^{201886}=1. \tag{15}
\]
Similarly,
\[
 \frac{N+1}{3}=201886\cdot3^{39100}. \tag{16}
\]
Thus equation (12) says
\[
 \theta^{(N+1)/3}=A+B\theta.
\]
By (13), \(B\) is invertible modulo \(N\). This verifies the second hypothesis of the proposition.

For the discriminant condition, with \(p=4\) we have
\[
 p^2-4=16-4=12.
\]
The integer \(N\) is odd, because \(201886\cdot3^{39101}\) is even and \(N\) is one less than it. Also \(N\equiv-1\pmod3\). Therefore \(N\) is divisible by neither 2 nor 3, and hence
\[
 \gcd(12,N)=1.
\]
Thus \(12\) is a unit modulo \(N\), as required.

Equation (14) immediately gives
\[
 3^{39101}\mid N+1.
\]
It remains only to check the size inequality. Write \(q=3^{39101}\). We need
\[
 201886q-1<(q-1)^2.
\]
The difference between the right and left sides is
\[
 (q-1)^2-(201886q-1)
 =q^2-201888q+2
 =q(q-201888)+2.
\]
Since
\[
 q=3^{39101}>3^{12}=531441>201888,
\]
this difference is positive. Hence
\[
 N<(3^{39101}-1)^2. \tag{17}
\]

All hypotheses of the proposition are now satisfied with \(p=4\) and \(m=39101\). Therefore
\[
 N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1
   =2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime.

## 5. Conclusion for A354747

For a positive integer \(n\), let
\[
 S_n=\{m\in\mathbb N:m\ge1\text{ and }2n\,3^m-1\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
The sequence value \(a(n)\) is the least member of \(S_n\) when this set is nonempty, and is defined to be 0 only when no such positive exponent exists.

We have proved that
\[
 39101\in S_{100943}.
\]
Thus \(S_{100943}\) is nonempty. Every member of this set is at least 1, so its least member is also at least 1. Consequently
\[
 a(100943)\neq0.
\]
Indeed, the argument gives the upper bound \(a(100943)\le39101\), though it does not need to identify the least successful exponent.

Therefore the conjecture
\[
 a(100943)=0
\]
is false.
